The archive is sparse and strongly concentrated at order 3: seven order-3 cells are filled, compared with three at order 2, one at order 4, and none in the searchable order-1 grid. Within order 3, held-out error generally improves as stage count and bucket increase, reaching 2.647e-02 at six stages in bucket 4. That cell also has the lowest recorded search error, 6.697e-03. The current cell is therefore aligned with the most favorable observed region, although most neighboring buckets remain unexplored.

The pattern is consistent with additional stages providing more freedom to satisfy order conditions while accommodating fixed-point coefficient constraints. The progression from three-stage buckets 2, 3 through six-stage bucket 4 also suggests that higher buckets may become accessible only after enough stages are available. Order alone does not explain performance: the sole order-4 entry has a held-out error of 7.851e-02, worse than every archived order-3 entry, so coefficient quality, quantization effects, and search convergence appear at least as relevant as formal order in the tested regime.

A substantial gap between search and held-out error appears throughout the archive. For example, the six-stage order-3 candidate rises from 6.697e-03 in search to 2.647e-02 when held out, while the four-stage order-2 candidate rises from 1.739e-02 to 8.301e-02. This could reflect optimization toward the search cases, sensitivity to the held-out problem distribution, or numerical effects that are not captured by the search objective. The supplied material contains no literature-digest text, so direct agreement with particular published constructions cannot be assessed; the broad tradeoff among order conditions, stage count, coefficient restrictions, and generalization is nevertheless the natural literature context for these observations.

No hypotheses are currently open or refuted, and the large number of empty cells makes boundary claims premature. The next useful examination is the local neighborhood around order 3 at five and six stages, especially buckets 3, 5, with repeated evaluations to determine whether the apparent improvement is stable. It would also be useful to populate comparable order-2 and order-4 cells, inspect per-problem held-out failures, and test whether the search-to-held-out gap persists under broader or differently weighted search cases.

The archive is still sparse and strongly concentrated in third-order methods: 8 of 32 third-order cells are filled, compared with 3 of 40 for order two and 1 of 24 for order four. No searchable earliest-order cell is occupied, although one result exists outside its stage range. Within the third-order entries, held-out error generally falls as stages and bucket increase, reaching 2.323e-02 at six stages, bucket 4, the best archived value. The current cell is this same stage, bucket location, so further activity there may refine an already favorable region rather than broaden coverage.

The pattern is consistent with a tradeoff between available stages, order constraints, and quantization. Extra stages appear useful for third-order schemes, but increasing formal order alone does not guarantee a smaller fixed-point error: the sole fourth-order entry has a held-out error of 7.851e-02, worse than every archived third-order entry. More order conditions and intermediate operations can restrict the feasible coefficient set and introduce additional rounding accumulation. The substantial gaps between search and held-out errors, sometimes by factors of roughly two to seven, also suggest that candidates can fit the search cases without transferring equally well to unseen cases.

The literature digest helps explain why performance need not follow the usual real-arithmetic hierarchy. Embedded pairs and higher-order formulas can be efficient in floating-point arithmetic, but Q15 error estimates may collapse to zero, while floor rounding systematically pushes discarded fractions downward. Repeated stage quantization can therefore offset benefits from smaller truncation terms. Likewise, PI or digital-filter control may smooth step sequences only when its integer definitions, saturation behavior, zero-error policy, and history state are well specified; rejection and lost FSAL reuse can also change both accuracy and bounded execution cost.

No hypotheses have yet accumulated a verdict, and the limited occupancy makes broad conclusions premature. In particular, the lone fourth-order result cannot establish whether fourth-order designs are generally disadvantaged, while empty high-bucket cells leave the effects of coefficient scale or representability largely unobserved. Useful next examinations include expanding coverage around third-order stages five and six, testing more fourth-order cells, measuring how often embedded differences quantize to zero, and separating truncation error from stage-rounding and controller-rounding effects. Recording rejection counts, FSAL validity, saturation events, and held-out behavior under alternative rounding policies would clarify which mechanism drives the observed generalization gaps.

The archive is sparse and strongly concentrated in order three: eight of its 32 searchable cells are filled, compared with three order-two cells and one order-four cell, while order one has no in-range entries. Within order three, the best held-out error is 2.323e-02 for six stages in bucket 4, followed by 2.748e-02 for five stages in the same bucket. Increasing stages is not uniformly beneficial, however: in bucket 3, five stages reaches 2.896e-02 while six stages reaches 3.204e-02. The current six-stage, bucket-4 cell is already occupied, and a stall counter of 25 suggests that recent work has not improved or broadened the archive.

The occupied cells show substantial gaps between search and held-out error. For example, the six-stage, bucket-4 order-three entry has search error 1.009e-02 but held-out error 2.323e-02, while the corresponding five-stage entry moves from 9.910e-03 to 2.748e-02. This may reflect tuning to the search cases, sensitivity to unseen spectra, or changes introduced by Q15 coefficients and floor-rounded stage arithmetic. The weak order-four result, with held-out error 7.851e-02, also illustrates that satisfying a higher formal order does not automatically produce better behavior under this discrete implementation and cost model.

These observations fit the literature digest’s account of the tradeoff between stage count, stability geometry, and cost. A sixth stage gives an order-three method additional freedom to reshape its stability polynomial, which could explain its advantage over five stages in bucket 4. Yet its 181 measured cycles exceed the five-stage entry’s 130 cycles, and the reversed ranking in bucket 3 shows that the benefit depends on the targeted regime rather than stage count alone. Comparisons should therefore emphasize stable progress or held-out accuracy per measured cycle, and should use the implemented fixed-point amplification map rather than infer behavior solely from floating-point stability regions.

The stated hypothesis remains observationally unresolved by this snapshot because it requires a particular crossover between fast and slow cost models, whereas the archive shown does not provide an explicit paired fast/slow comparison. The most useful next examination is a direct five-versus-six-stage evaluation on identical held-out spectra under both cost models, including admissible step size, error per cycle, overflow or saturation behavior, and fixed-point amplification near stability boundaries. Replicating the occupied bucket-3 and bucket-4 comparisons and probing neighboring empty cells would help distinguish a persistent stage-count effect from bucket-specific tuning or search variance.

The archive is sparse and strongly concentrated at order 3. Eight of 32 order-3 cells are occupied, compared with three order-2 cells and one order-4 cell; no searchable order-1 cell is filled. Within order 3, the best held-out error improves from 3.922e-02 at three stages to 3.363e-02 at four, 2.516e-02 at five, and 2.323e-02 at six. These entries also move toward higher cost buckets, so the apparent gain accompanies added stages and computational cost rather than isolating either effect.

Search error and held-out error are not tightly aligned. The four-stage order-3 entry in bucket 3 has the lowest search error in the archive, 2.769e-03, but its held-out error is 3.363e-02; the six-stage bucket-4 entry has a higher search error of 1.009e-02 yet the best held-out result. Similar gaps occur elsewhere, especially for the order-2 and order-4 entries. This suggests that optimization on the search cases can over-specialize coefficients, while stage count, bucket constraints, stability behavior, or the composition of the held-out problems affects generalization.

The resolved hypothesis provides a more specific caution about attributing performance to cost models. The proposed reversal between five- and six-stage order-3 methods under slow- and fast-cost assumptions was not observed, despite 2,687 samples and a moderate reported effect size of 0.381. The archive therefore supports describing the six-stage bucket-4 candidate as better than the five-stage bucket-4 candidate in the displayed held-out measurements, but not as evidence for a cost-model-dependent ranking reversal. This fits the usual literature emphasis on separating formal order, stage cost, stability properties, and empirical accuracy; no literature-digest details are included here, so a closer comparison with particular published mechanisms is not possible from this snapshot alone.

Substantial uncertainty remains because most grid cells are empty, the run has stalled for 20 cycles, and the current six-stage bucket-4 cell may have received more search effort than many alternatives. The next useful checks are repeated held-out evaluation across problem families and step sizes, matched-search-budget comparisons between five and six stages, and examination of coefficient quantization, stability regions, and error constants. Filling nearby order-3 buckets and more order-4 cells would help distinguish a genuine stage-related trend from uneven coverage or selection effects.

The archive remains sparse after 449 cycles, with 12 searchable cells occupied overall and no searchable order-1 entries. Order 3 has the broadest coverage and the lowest held-out errors: its best entry is the six-stage, bucket-4 cell at 2.323e-02, followed closely by the five-stage, bucket-4 cell at 2.516e-02. Order 2 is represented in only three cells, all with held-out errors above 5.3e-02, while the sole order-4 entry has 7.851e-02. Thus the present pattern favors the explored order-3 region, but the many empty cells make comparisons across orders and cost buckets incomplete.

Increasing the number of stages appears useful only in combination with the right cost bucket. Within order 3, the stronger results move from buckets 2, 3 at three and four stages toward buckets 3, 4 at five and six stages. More stages may provide additional coefficient freedom, while a larger bucket may admit coefficient encodings that approximate the desired tableau more accurately. The sizable gaps between search and held-out error, especially the five-stage bucket-4 result of 3.002e-03 versus 2.516e-02, also suggest that search-set fit is not a reliable proxy for generalization. The recorded samples did not exhibit the proposed slow-cost versus fast-cost ranking reversal between the five- and six-stage order-3 cells; the observed relationship therefore cannot be explained by that crossover as stated.

The literature digest gives a plausible reason for sensitivity to the cost model. On Cortex-M0+, multiplication may take either one or 32 cycles depending on the implementation, whereas shifts, additions, and subtractions are nominally single-cycle under zero-wait-state assumptions. CSD weight can approximate the cost of multiplierless constant products, but it does not capture shared intermediates, factored shift-add graphs, dependency depth, compiler choices, or memory stalls. Bucket membership based on a simplified constant-cost metric may therefore group methods whose realized execution costs differ, and it may obscure useful tableau-wide sharing among coefficients.

The largest uncertainty is coverage: nearly all order-2 and order-4 cells remain empty, as do the outer cost buckets for order 3, and the current six-stage bucket-3 cell has not yet been filled despite the search being positioned there. The stall counter of five may indicate difficulty finding feasible candidates locally rather than absence of good methods. Useful next examinations include completing nearby order-3 cells, repeating evaluations to quantify held-out variability, and inspecting why search error sometimes understates held-out error so sharply. For hardware-facing conclusions, the candidate methods should also be compiled or explicitly scheduled for a named Cortex-M0+ multiplier configuration, with instruction counts, shared shift-add expressions, dependency chains, and memory wait states measured separately.

The lowest held-out error is 2.323e-02 for the six-stage, order-3 method in bucket 4, followed closely by 2.516e-02 for five stages in the same bucket. Within the populated order-3 region, held-out error generally improves toward five or six stages and buckets 3, 4, although the pattern is not perfectly monotone. The current six-stage, bucket-4 cell remains empty for orders 1, 2, and 4, and a stall counter of 10 indicates that recent work has not expanded coverage.

Search error is consistently lower than held-out error, sometimes by a wide margin. For example, the five-stage, order-3 bucket-4 entry has a search error of 3.002e-03 but a held-out error of 2.516e-02. This gap suggests that selection on the search cases can favor coefficient sets whose fixed-point behavior does not transfer uniformly to other trajectories or step regimes. The extra stages available to the stronger order-3 entries may reduce truncation error or provide more favorable coefficient structure, but they also introduce more quantized operations and more opportunities for biased floor-rounding errors to accumulate.

That tradeoff matches the literature digest: reducing discretization error does not guarantee lower long-run error once quantization, stage-level amplification, drift, and update stagnation become significant. Because Q15 floor rounding is directed, the usual square-root accumulation picture for unbiased stochastic rounding is not directly applicable; coherent drift may help explain why held-out performance remains substantially worse than search performance. The digest also cautions that algebraically equivalent Runge, Kutta implementations can amplify internal errors differently, so stage count and formal order alone cannot explain the archive.

The recorded six-stage versus five-stage order-3 comparison did not exhibit the proposed reversal between the slow- and fast-cost models; its resolved sample showed a moderate standardized separation, with Cohen’s d about 0.381. It remains unclear whether the sparse higher-order coverage reflects genuine feasibility limits, the search allocation, coefficient quantization, or difficulty reaching the relevant buckets. Useful next examinations include decomposing held-out error into truncation, systematic drift, stagnated updates, and stage-error amplification; testing alternative implementations of the same tableaux; and collecting more results around order 3, stages 5, 6, buckets 3, 5 before interpreting neighboring empty cells as evidence of absence.

These patterns fit the literature digest’s distinction between classical Runge, Kutta quality and fixed-point implementation quality. Extra stages create degrees of freedom that can improve a secondary objective, but they also introduce more rounded stage operations and more routes for internal perturbations to propagate. Consequently, order conditions, principal-error norms, or an optimized stability polynomial alone would not explain the observed rankings. The resolved H-006 observation is recorded as refuted with a moderate positive effect size of 0.381: the proposed reversal between the slow- and fast-cost models was not supported by the sampled results, even though the archived aggregate minima show six stages slightly ahead of five in bucket 4.

The main uncertainty is whether empty cells reflect genuine infeasibility, insufficient exploration, or difficulty satisfying constraints under the fixed-point representation. The lone order-4 result has relatively high held-out error, but one cell cannot establish an order-level trend. Useful next checks are repeated evaluations of the order-3 five- and six-stage bucket-4 candidates, direct comparison of their internal-stability amplification and rounding trajectories, and exact or high-precision verification of their order-condition residuals. Broader sampling around adjacent buckets would also show whether the six-stage advantage is stable or merely a consequence of uneven archive coverage and candidate selection.

These patterns agree with the literature digest’s emphasis on realized arithmetic structure rather than classical order or stage count alone. Fixed-point performance depends on coefficient representation, shift opportunities, intermediate ranges, rounding, and the resulting instruction schedule. A longer method can therefore achieve better numerical behavior without necessarily being preferable in every cost regime, while a higher formal order can perform poorly if its coefficients or internal stages interact badly with quantization. The isolated order-4 result and the non-monotone order-3 comparisons are consistent with that mechanism, although the FPGA resource reductions reported for optimized RK4 implementations cannot be transferred directly to Q15 arithmetic or Cortex-M0+ cycle costs.

The main uncertainty is coverage: one order-4 cell, three order-2 cells, and no searchable order-1 cells are insufficient for broad comparisons among orders, stages, and cost buckets. It would be useful to examine the empty order-3 cells adjacent to the current region, repeat the five- versus six-stage comparison across matched buckets and cost models, and inspect the tableaux for powers-of-two coefficients, accumulator range, saturation, and floor-rounding bias. Reporting error distributions rather than only best values would also show whether the apparent gains are stable across held-out problems or driven by a small subset of cases.

The order-3 results show that stage count alone does not determine quality. Moving toward buckets 3 and 4 generally coincides with lower errors, but the benefit varies by stage count and evaluation set. Search errors are uniformly below held-out errors, sometimes by a wide margin: the five-stage, bucket-4 entry has search error 3.002e-03 but held-out error 2.516e-02. This gap is consistent with selection pressure favoring tableaus that fit the search cases or objective particularly well without transferring proportionally to held-out cases. The larger cycle counts in the stronger order-3 cells also suggest that finding useful coefficients in these regions requires substantially more optimization effort.

These patterns fit the literature digest’s description of Runge, Kutta construction as a nonlinear constrained polynomial search with many local solutions. Once the rooted-tree order conditions are satisfied, additional stages provide free parameters, but those parameters can improve a principal error norm, stability behavior, cost, or implementation properties in different and potentially competing ways. That helps explain why extra stages sometimes improve held-out error and sometimes do not, and why rankings can depend on the cost model. The refuted ranking-reversal hypothesis is therefore best read as an observed absence of that specific conjunction in 2,687 samples, not as evidence that stage count and cost modeling are generally unrelated.

Substantial uncertainty remains because most cells are empty, order 4 has only one representative, and the archive reports best occupants rather than the distribution or variability of attempted solutions. The most useful next examination would be denser sampling around the order-3 bucket-3 and bucket-4 frontier, especially paired five- and six-stage searches under both cost models, with repeated starts to separate persistent structure from local-optimizer effects. It would also help to decompose the objective into next-order rooted-tree residuals, stability measures, and internal-error amplification, since similar aggregate search errors may conceal different numerical mechanisms and implementation sensitivity.

The archive is still sparse: 14 searchable cells are filled, with no searchable order-1 entries, only one order-4 entry, and the search currently stalled at the five-stage, bucket-4 cell. Order 3 provides the clearest pattern. Moving toward higher-cost buckets generally lowers held-out error, and the best recorded value is 2.323e-02 for the six-stage, bucket-4 method. The comparable five-stage, bucket-4 method is slightly worse at 2.516e-02, while both improve substantially over lower-bucket entries. Extra stages alone do not guarantee improvement, however; comparisons also depend on bucket and coefficient choice.

Held-out errors are consistently higher than search errors, sometimes by large factors. This suggests that optimization is exploiting the finite search workload and that coefficient quantization, saturation, floor rounding, or workload-specific dynamics limit transfer to held-out cases. The additional cycle cost associated with better order-3 entries is also visible: the strongest held-out results require roughly 125, 181 cycles, compared with about 61, 68 cycles for the three-stage entries. The archived observation behind H-006 did not show the proposed cost-model ranking reversal; although its effect-size estimate is positive and moderate, the required conjunction was not observed across 2,687 samples.

These patterns fit the literature digest’s broader accuracy-versus-bounded-work tension. Fixed-stage explicit methods provide deterministic execution, while higher accuracy or conservation-oriented methods often require implicit solves, relaxation steps, or other nontrivial work. At the same time, the archive reinforces the warning that reduced precision does not automatically deliver a favorable speed, accuracy tradeoff: Q15 coefficient truncation and asymmetric floor rounding can alter both local error and stability behavior. Conservation results from real-valued or differently rounded schemes therefore cannot be assumed to carry over to this implementation.

The many empty cells make broad conclusions premature, especially for orders 1, 2, and 4 and for high buckets. It is also unclear whether the search-to-held-out gaps arise mainly from overfitting, altered stability regions, saturation events, or systematic rounding bias. Useful next examinations include filling nearby order-3 cells to test whether the bucket trend persists, revisiting the five- versus six-stage comparison under both cost models, recording saturation and rounding-error statistics, and probing stability and invariant drift on held-out problems. Replicated evaluations around the best order-3 cells would help distinguish robust performance differences from sensitivity to particular workloads or coefficient choices.

Within order 3, moving toward higher buckets and adding stages generally coincides with lower held-out error, but the pattern is not monotone. Six stages improves on five stages in bucket 4, whereas five stages is better in bucket 3. This interaction helps explain why H-006 was refuted: the proposed reversal between slow- and fast-cost rankings is not supported by the sampled archive. The moderate reported effect size indicates a detectable ranking difference, but not the specific conjunction stated by the hypothesis.

Search error is consistently lower than held-out error, sometimes by a wide margin. For example, the order-3 five-stage bucket-4 candidate has search error 3.002e-03 but held-out error 2.516e-02. This suggests that optimization on the search cases can exploit case-specific structure and that held-out evaluation is materially constraining the apparent quality of candidates. The higher cycle counts in the stronger order-3 cells may also reflect that useful coefficients are harder to locate in those regions rather than arising simply from additional stages.

No literature digest content is included in the supplied data, so a direct comparison with published mechanisms or expected stage, order tradeoffs cannot be made here. The large number of empty cells also leaves uncertainty about whether the visible trends reflect the method family or the search trajectory; the current six-stage bucket-3 cell and the stall counter of two make that especially relevant. The next useful examination is denser coverage around order 3, stages 5, 6, buckets 3, 5, with repeated searches and matched cost settings, followed by targeted exploration of order 4 to determine whether its single weak entry is representative or merely undersampled.

The large gaps between search and held-out errors also indicate that search-set fit is an unreliable proxy for generalization.

The observed structure is consistent with interacting discretization and quantization effects. More stages and higher order can reduce truncation error, but they also introduce additional fixed-point products, sums, coefficient approximations, and opportunities for floor-rounding bias or saturation. Bucket changes may alter this balance more than stage count itself. The current six-stage, bucket-4 cell has accumulated 181 cycles, yet the run has stalled for 19 cycles, suggesting that local refinement is no longer producing archive improvements readily.

The recorded comparison associated with H-006 does not exhibit the proposed slow-versus-fast ranking reversal. Its positive effect size of about 0.38 indicates a measurable difference across 2,687 samples, but the archive summary does not expose the slow- and fast-cost results separately, so the direction and practical size of each component cannot be reconstructed here. More broadly, the weak order-4 result and absence of higher-order coverage do not establish that higher formal order is unsuitable; they may instead reflect limited exploration, difficult coefficient quantization, or controller behavior.

This aligns with the literature digest’s warning that familiar embedded-pair advantages do not transfer automatically to Q15 arithmetic. Embedded estimates and PI or digital-filter control require integer definitions for normalization, scaling, clamping, rounding, overflow, and rejection, and those choices can dominate the expected stage-count and order tradeoffs. The next useful examination is therefore to separate integration error from controller and arithmetic effects: compare five- and six-stage order-3 candidates under identical cost models, inspect saturation and rejection traces, measure rounding bias by stage, and test nearby empty buckets. Broader exploration of order 4 and the unfilled six-stage cells is also needed before interpreting the present concentration as a stable property of the search space.

The archive is sparse and strongly concentrated in order three: nine order-3 cells are filled, compared with five at order two, one at order four, and none within the searchable range at order one. Among recorded candidates, the lowest held-out error is 2.320e-02 for the six-stage, order-3 method in bucket 4, followed closely by the five-stage bucket-4 method at 2.516e-02. Adding stages generally helps within the populated order-3 region, although the pattern is not monotone across every bucket. The current six-stage bucket-4 cell is therefore the strongest recorded point, but the stall counter of nine and the many empty cells indicate that archive coverage remains limited.

Search errors are consistently below held-out errors, sometimes by a wide margin. For example, the four-stage, order-3 bucket-2 candidate has search error 3.669e-03 but held-out error 4.283e-02, while the five-stage bucket-4 candidate moves from 3.002e-03 to 2.516e-02. This suggests substantial specialization to the search cases, with fixed-point rounding, stage iteration behavior, or a narrow training workload producing solutions that transfer imperfectly. The lone order-4 entry performs worse than all archived order-3 entries despite its higher formal order, which is compatible with finite-precision and finite-iteration effects overwhelming the asymptotic advantage of the underlying RK formula.

The recorded data do not exhibit the proposed slow-cost versus fast-cost reversal between the five- and six-stage order-3 cells; the associated comparison was resolved earlier from 2,687 samples with a moderate standardized separation. The literature digest offers several mechanisms for such cost-dependent behavior without guaranteeing it: sequential SDIRK stages and reusable diagonals can reduce repeated work, whereas coupled Radau stages incur different solve costs, and Rosenbrock methods replace nonlinear solves with linear ones that may share a factorization. On Cortex-M0+, multiplier latency, widening, scaling, saturation, division, and iteration counts can all change the practical ranking. A fixed iteration cap also changes the realized method unless the coefficients and iteration scheme were designed together, so formal RK order alone is not enough to predict these measurements.

The largest uncertainty is the amount of missing coverage, especially for order four, all six-stage order-two cells, and the outer cost buckets. It is also unclear how much of the held-out gap comes from coefficient selection versus Q15 floor rounding, premature iteration termination, saturation, or nonconvergence on particular cases. Useful next examinations are repeated held-out evaluation of the leading order-3 cells, per-case error and convergence traces, and cycle accounting separated into multiplication, division, scaling, and nonlinear iterations. Filling nearby empty cells, particularly five- and six-stage order-3 buckets 5 through 7 and additional order-4 cells, would show whether the current concentration around bucket 4 is a persistent frontier or an artifact of incomplete search.

The archive is sparse and strongly concentrated in orders 2 and 3. Order 3 currently gives the lowest held-out errors, improving from about 3.92e-2 at three stages to 2.32e-2 at six stages, with the best entries shifting toward higher cost buckets as stages increase. Order 2 does not show the same benefit from additional stages: its three-stage results are best at roughly 4.36e-2, while the populated four- and five-stage cells are worse. The lone order-4 entry has a comparatively high held-out error of 7.85e-2, and no searchable order-1 cell is filled.

The large gaps between search and held-out errors suggest that optimizing against the search workload does not reliably predict performance on the held-out workload. This is especially visible in order-3 cells such as five stages, bucket 4, where a search error of 3.00e-3 corresponds to a held-out error of 2.52e-2. More stages can reduce truncation error or provide useful coefficient freedom, but they also introduce more fixed-point multiplications, additions, shifts, and opportunities for saturation.
